edits.quote: Fill the sailboat.
edits.fix: A single fill of an 11-triangle outline is done in a minute and has no question. Give it a real goal: fill the sailboat in several different ways, then with the fewest pieces you can, then try it with only blue pieces (impossible: 11 triangles; the sail alone leaves 2 gaps).

edits.quote: Use any small pieces.
edits.fix: 'Small' is ambiguous (regular vs. upscale blocks, or 'small' = triangles), and pink, teal and gray pieces do not fit this grid. Name the allowed pieces: green triangles, blue rhombi, red trapezoids.

edits.quote: Sailboat
edits.fix: Delete the caption above the diagram; the problem text already names the shape.

edits.quote: Sailboat outline with nothing to record on; lower 60% of the page blank
edits.fix: Add recording space: small copies of the sailboat to trace or color each filling, and a box for the number of pieces used.

edits.quote: Cover the mountain with green triangles. How many did you use?
edits.fix: This is routine counting to 9. Rewrite it as the K-1 entry to the outline's kernel 1: cover the mountain with as few pieces as you can, then with only blue pieces. How many triangle spaces stay uncovered, and can anyone leave fewer? (At least 3: 6 up-triangles and 3 down-triangles.)

edits.quote: Mountain
edits.fix: Delete the caption above the diagram.

edits.quote: How many did you use?
edits.fix: Add an answer box next to the question.

edits.quote: Worksheet ends after two short problems (about 5 minutes for a quick child)
edits.fix: Add substantial K-1 work at actual size. Example: one shape (such as the yellow hexagon outline or a 2x upscale triangle) filled in as many different ways as possible, with recording outlines.

edits.quote: Still roughly 20 more minutes missing for a quick child
edits.fix: Add contrasting boards that blue rhombi can and cannot fill (an even-area shape with more up- than down-triangles), and a growing-triangle problem: how many greens cover the 2x and 3x triangles.

k-1.summary: Two pages with one trivial fill and one count-to-nine; the drawings are correct and at actual size, but there is no mathematical idea and no recording space. A quick child is done in about five minutes, which is exactly the organizer's complaint that K-1 is dumbed down and ends too early. The band needs a rewrite around kernel 1 at a concrete entry point.

edits.quote: Boards A-D: A is a 3-edge triangle (9 triangles), B a 2x3 parallelogram (12), C an 11-triangle shape, D a 10-triangle hexagon
edits.fix: The only impossible boards (A and C) have an odd number of triangles, so the sole obstruction children meet is 'odd count'. The kernel's point, even area but more up- than down-triangles, never appears. Replace C (or A) with an even-area board with unequal counts, e.g. the trapezoid 4 edges along the bottom, 2 on top, 2 rows tall (12 triangles: 7 up, 5 down).

edits.quote: Each blue covers two whole triangle spaces. Keep pieces inside the board without overlaps. / (P2) without overlaps or pieces outside
edits.fix: State the activity-wide rule once, as a short shared rule at the top: pieces sit exactly on triangle spaces, inside the board, with no overlaps. Remove the repeats from P1 and P2. 'Each blue covers two whole triangle spaces' also hands children the counting argument.

edits.quote: Which boards can you fill and which ones did you get stuck on? What is stopping you from completely filling some of the shapes?
edits.fix: Rewrite as one clear task: 'Which boards can be filled? For each board that cannot, explain why not.' Put a short answer space under each board instead of two shared lines.

edits.quote: on these triangles and the triangle on the next page
edits.fix: There is no next page; all three triangles are on this page. Delete 'and the triangle on the next page'.

edits.quote: Fit as many as you can, without overlaps or pieces outside. Record how many blues fit and how many triangle spaces stay empty.
edits.fix: The problem stops at recording, so a child cannot tell when they are done and the kernel's lower-bound argument is never asked for. Add: 'Could anyone leave fewer empty spaces? Explain why not. How many would stay empty on a triangle with 10 small edges on each side?' (Answers: 2, 3, 4 empty; 10.)

edits.quote: Packet ends after P2 (about 15 minutes for a quick child)
edits.fix: Add a problem of contrasting even-area boards (balanced and unbalanced, e.g. a hexagon with a corner triangle moved) where children predict, then test, whether blues can fill them.

edits.quote: Still roughly 10-15 minutes missing
edits.fix: Add a fewest-gaps problem with the purple chevron (can it beat the blues on the 4-edge triangle?), or have children design a board with an even number of triangles that blues cannot fill.

grades-2-3.summary: Boards are correctly drawn at actual size and P2 holds the kernel's real pattern (n gaps on an n-edge triangle). But both impossible boards in P1 fail only by odd area, and P2 never asks why fewer gaps are impossible, so the coloring idea goes unprompted. With two problems it runs about fifteen minutes for a quick child; it needs a corrected P1, the 'why' question, and roughly 25 more minutes of work.

edits.quote: Find as many different tilings as you can.
edits.fix: There is no end condition, and the 8 recording boards invite a hunt for 8. Use 'Find all the tilings. How do you know you have them all?' (There are 6.)

edits.quote: Six cards A-F showing every tiling of the hexagon
edits.fix: Page 2 prints all six tilings, which gives away P1's answer if children see it early. Either have children letter their own recordings from P1 and draw the map on those, or tell the adult to hand out page 2 only after P1.

edits.quote: line joining the centers of its two trian- gle spaces.
edits.fix: Widen the side-note box or turn off hyphenation so 'triangle' is not split.

edits.quote: Find the shortest route from A to F. Write the cards you visit and count your flips.
edits.fix: There are two shortest routes (A-B-C-E-F and A-B-D-E-F, 4 flips each), so 'the' route is ill-posed, and once the map is drawn this is a one-minute lookup. Ask: 'Find every shortest route from A to F. Which two cards are the most flips apart?'

edits.quote: Explain what you notice.
edits.fix: Replace with 'Explain why.'

edits.quote: Cross its rhombus to the middle of its opposite horizontal edge. Keep crossing upward until you reach the top. Follow the example on A, then draw the ribbon on B.
edits.fix: The dashed example on A already shows the procedure. Cut to one sentence defining the ribbon and the L/R code, and let the example carry the rest.

edits.quote: At any step, is there a choice of which rhombus to cross next? Could one tiling have two different ribbons starting at the bold edge?
edits.fix: These are low-value follow-ups, and the second only restates the first. Delete them and use the space for the payoff questions (next edit).

edits.quote: P5 asks only for the code of one tiling (B); P4 asks for an explanation before ribbons exist
edits.fix: Add the kernel's payoff: write the code of every card (RRLL, RLRL, LRRL, RLLR, LRLR, LLRR); notice each has two L's and two R's and every arrangement appears once, so there are exactly 6 tilings; and see what one flip does to a code (it swaps a neighboring L and R). Move P4 after P5 so the codes can explain why round trips take an even number of flips.

edits.quote: Labels 'A' and 'B' above the P5 ribbon diagrams overlap the hexagons' top edges
edits.fix: Move the labels up so they clear the outlines.

edits.quote: A quick child is out of substantial tasks after about 28 minutes; the bottom third of page 3 is empty
edits.fix: Add a larger actual-size hexagon (1 edge on the bottom, sides of 2 and 3; 22 triangles, 11 blues). Children predict the number of tilings from ribbon codes (10), then check some with blocks.

grades-4-5.summary: This is the strongest band: the 1-2-2 hexagon and all six cards are drawn correctly, the shown flip is a real flip, the map is the right graph, and the odd-round-trip question has a real answer. It falls short at the end: P3 is a one-minute lookup with two answers, and the ribbon problem stops before its payoff (codes count the tilings and explain the parity of flips). It needs the payoff, a resequenced P4, and about ten more minutes of work.

overall.strongest: The grades 4-5 pages develop the outline's flip-graph kernel through a correct, well-drawn sequence: all six tilings, an accurate flip map, and a real parity question.
overall.weakest: The K-1 pages are one trivial fill and one count-to-nine that a quick child finishes in about five minutes, with no mathematical idea; this is the organizer's 'dumbed down and ends too early' complaint exactly.
